
# Filling in the Details {#sec-details}

With a simplified case understood, and some key metaphors and visuals for understanding the process, we can start to add back in features until we have parity with the current Actual Budget algorithm.

## Gradual and Immediate Templates

Not all templates are of the gradual type. Most specify an amount to add to the budget in this month, not a target balance for a future date. We'll call these Immediate templates to contrast with the Gradual templates. No complicated math is needed to determine the contribution amount for an immedaite template, but we have to be careful when combining gradual and immedate in the same category or we could lose the desireable properties we want the algorithm to have.

The approach we'll take is to first apply the gradual templates, then the immediate templates. 

[Why? Immediate templates come with the assumption of spending in that month. When applying after, we get consistent contributions and the immediate templates/spending kind of "cancel out" on top of it. Show example and table. Refer to appendix for alternative.]{style="color:red;"}

### Translating Templates {.unnumbered}

So far, we've just been talking about Gradual and Immediate templates, but these are not the terms used by Actual Budget. We need a system to translate Actual Budget's template types to either Gradual or Immediate for use in this algorithm.

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
**Immediate**

* Simple Type
* Periodic Type
* Percent Type
* Schedule Type (with `full` flag)
* Average Type
* Copy Type
:::

::: {.column}
**Gradual**

* By Type
* Schedule Type (without `full` flag)
:::
:::::

Remainder Type templates are considered separately, after all other templates have run, as they are now. Limits on categories (i.e. `up to`) function the same as they do now, also.

## Spend From

:::{style="color:red;"}
After determining which transactions apply for the template, subtract their total from the goal. Why? Assumption is that any spending is from balance already contributed, therefore only total minus spending is needed for rest of goal.

## Priorities

So far, the algorithm works with groups of templates as a whole, not individual templates. And for long-term templates, it's not possible to work out the contribution due to one template or another. So to implement priorities we need to work backwards. If $T_1,\dots,T_n$ are templates sorted in order of priority, and $C(\dots)$ is the function that returns the total contribution required by a specific set of templates, then the incremental effect of the last template, $T_n$, is given by the difference between the contribution amounts with and without $T_n$.

$$C(T_1,\dots,T_{n-1},T_n) - C(T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}),$$ {#eq-priorities-generic}

This idea is pretty flexible, and can be used for any function $C$, not just this specific algorithm. So different long-term templates in the same category can be given different priorities, and the incremental effect of each template can be found easily. When working with templates of different priorities, we can continue until we reach a $n^\ast$ where $C(T_1,\dots,T_{n^\ast})$ is greater than the available funds to spend, at which point $T_{n^\ast-1}$ is the last template to succeed, $T_{n^\ast}$ could partially succeed, and any $T_n$ with $n > n^\ast$ will fail.

One thing that is a little weird about this approach is that the amount contributed due to a template could be different depending on its position in the priority order. For example in @exm-multiple-by, if the last template, `#template 100 by 2026-10` is the highest priority template, then it is responsible for \$14.29 of contribution. But if it is the lowest priority template, then it is responsible for \$0 of contribution. But the total contribution from all three templates is the same no matter the priority order of the templates. So if you have \$120 of available funds, all three templates will succeed no matter their order. But if you have less than \$120, the priority order would affect which templates succeed and which fail, as expected.
